subsection: 1. Roles and responsibilities in the family

notes.h: Family life cycle and changing roles
notes.b: A family is not the same from one decade to the next. It passes through stages, and each stage changes who does what and how heavy the workload is. A role is the pattern of behaviour expected of a person in a position such as parent or child, and a responsibility is a duty that goes with that role.
points: 1. Couple (establishment) stage: partners set up a shared home and divide household tasks, often according to paid work, time and skills.
2. Childbearing (expanding) stage: parents take on the provider, nurturing, educating and socialising roles for the first time, and the workload is at its peak.

3. Child-rearing stage (children of school age and adolescents): parents keep these roles while children take on more household tasks and independent responsibilities, and parents move from direct control towards guidance.
4. Launching stage: grown children leave home, so parents' roles change from daily care to advice and support at a distance, and the workload eases.

5. Later life stage (a retired couple, or one partner alone): older members may move from giving care to needing it, and adult children often take on practical, financial and emotional support for them.

Roles are not fixed. They are shaped by the stage the family is in, by each member's age, health, paid work and skills, and by social attitudes. Textbooks label the stages slightly differently, so describe each one as well as naming it.
notes.tip: Give the stages in order and name the main roles and demands of each. Workload and responsibility are highest in the childbearing and child-rearing stages, so say that when you describe how roles change.

notes.b: Parents carry a bundle of different roles at once. These roles can be shared between two parents or carried by one, and they matter because a parent who fills them well, with firm and fair explained rules, gives children the best start.
points: Provider: supplying food, clothing, shelter and money for the family's needs.
Nurturer: giving love, affection and emotional security, so that children feel safe and valued.
Educator: teaching skills, language, values and good habits through daily routines and example.
Socialiser: introducing children to the norms, beliefs and behaviour expected in family and community, so they learn how to get on with others.
Protector: ensuring safety, supervising children and making decisions in their best interests.
Manager: planning the household budget, meals, schedules and maintenance of the home.
Disciplinarian: setting boundaries and consequences that are explained and applied consistently, because children cope better with rules they understand.
notes.tip: You only need three or four of these roles, each with a short explanation of what the parent does. Provider, nurturer, educator, socialiser and protector are the points examiners expect, and you can add that parents now share these roles more and fathers are more involved in childcare.

notes.h: Roles of adolescents in the family
notes.b: Adolescents are not just receivers of care. As they grow, they take on real roles and responsibilities that prepare them for adult life, and these are best treated as growing responsibility rather than just chores.
points: Contributing to the household: helping with cooking, cleaning, shopping and minding younger siblings, so the workload is shared and parents have more time.
Managing their own schoolwork, timekeeping and personal belongings, which builds the self-discipline they will need as adults.
Developing independence: making decisions about friends, leisure and part-time work within agreed limits, so freedom grows alongside trust.
Respecting family rules and the privacy of others in shared space, so that everyone in the home can live together comfortably.
Sharing in family decisions, such as holidays or how to spend leisure time, which gives them a voice in family life.
Some adolescents earn money through part-time work, or give informal care to a sibling or grandparent.
notes.tip: Answers should name roles and responsibilities, not generic teenage needs. Aim for three or four roles, each with an explanation: contributing to the home, independence, schoolwork and respect for others.

notes.b: Who does what in a family has long depended on whether a person is male or female. These expectations have changed a great deal, but they have not disappeared.
points: Traditional segregated roles (separate, with each partner's tasks kept apart) assigned men as breadwinners and women as homemakers and primary carers of children. The father earned and the mother ran the home, in contrast to joint roles, where partners share tasks.

Where women work outside the home, they often still carry the larger share of domestic work and childcare, a pattern called the double shift, or second shift (a paid job followed by unpaid work at home).
Men's roles have expanded to include direct childcare, cooking and shared decision-making, and some fathers take the primary caring role.
Gender stereotypes can limit children's roles and experience, for example expecting girls to help in the kitchen and boys to do outdoor jobs.
Sharing household tasks equally reduces overload and resentment, and gives children a model of shared responsibility.
Adult daughters often take on more of the care of ageing parents than sons do.
notes.tip: Contrast the traditional division of work with the current one, and say who carries the unpaid load. Stereotyping and equality in the home are also asked about.

notes.h: Social and economic factors changing family roles (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Family roles have shifted a lot in recent times because society, money and technology have all changed. Each factor below matters because it changes who earns, who cares and who does the housework.
points: Women's participation in paid employment has increased, so many households depend on two earners and domestic roles have had to be shared. Greater gender equality and changed attitudes support this.
Lone-parent families have increased, so one adult often carries the provider, carer and household roles alone.
Smaller families, by choice or because of later marriage and childbearing, mean each child receives more parental time and money.
Greater acceptance of cohabitation, separation, divorce and blended families has created new parenting roles, such as step-parent.
Weaker extended-family and community support means parents have fewer relatives and neighbours to share childcare and other tasks.

Longer life expectancy means some families care for parents or grandparents while still raising children, a pattern called the sandwich generation (adults caught between caring for children and ageing parents at once).

Rising housing, childcare and education costs make two incomes necessary for many households, shifting the provider role to both partners. Unemployment can also reverse traditional provider and carer roles.

Longer working hours and commuting reduce the time available for family meals, shared activities and housework. Labour-saving appliances cut housework time so tasks can be divided differently, while mobile phones and the internet allow remote working and contact but also blur work and home time.
notes.tip: Name the factor, then state its effect on roles: for example, dual earners lead to shared housework and paid childcare, and lone parents carry all roles. Aim for four or five points, with at least one social and one economic.

notes.b: Role conflict arises when the demands of two or more roles held by one person cannot be met at the same time. It is common in modern families, where one adult may be a worker, parent, partner and carer all at once.
points: Work-family conflict: a parent is needed at work during the hours a child is ill or has a school event.
Role overload: one person carries too many responsibilities, such as employee, parent, carer and homemaker, for the time available.
Conflict between partners over who does which tasks, or whose career takes priority.
Intergenerational conflict: an adult may have to care for an older parent while still raising children at home.
Consequences include fatigue, stress, less quality time with the family, reduced quality of parenting, tension between partners and guilt.
Reducing conflict: explicit agreement on the division of tasks, flexible working arrangements, shared decision-making and help from extended family or services, such as childcare.
notes.tip: Role conflict is one person pulled between many roles. It is not the same as a clash between two people, such as an adolescent and a parent, so do not mix them up. Give examples and ways to reduce it.

notes.h: Investigating how family roles have changed
notes.b: One way to see how roles have changed is a short case study or interview with an older person, asking about family life fifty to one hundred years ago. A planned set of questions gives you something to compare with family life today.
points: 1. Decide who to interview, such as a grandparent or an older neighbour, and agree a time, so they are ready to talk.
2. Ask who earned the money in the family and who cared for the children, to show the provider and carer roles at that time.
3. Ask who did the housework and what tasks children were expected to do, to show how household work was divided.
4. Ask about family size, since the number of children affects how much care and work each person carried.
5. Record the answers accurately in your own notes, and write up only what the person told you, with no invented findings.
6. Compare the answers with family life today, looking for the kinds of change expected: more women in paid work, smaller families, shared tasks, labour-saving appliances and more mobile adolescents.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of stages a family passes through, from couple to childbearing, child-rearing, launching and later life, each with different roles and demands.
The parental responsibility to supply the food, clothing, shelter and money the family needs.
The process through which family members learn language, values, norms and the behaviour expected in their society.
A traditional division of family tasks by gender, with men as breadwinners and women as homemakers and carers.
A household in which both partners are in paid employment.
A family in which one parent has sole day-to-day responsibility for the children.
A clash between the demands of two or more roles held by one person that cannot all be met at the same time.
A situation in which one person has more responsibilities than the time or resources available allow them to fulfil.
Adults who care for ageing parents while also raising or supporting their own children.

factCards.term: Three social factors that have changed family roles
factCards.definition: Increased paid work by women, growth in lone-parent families, and smaller families.

factCards.term: Two economic factors that have changed family roles
factCards.definition: Rising housing and childcare costs that make two incomes necessary, and the longer working hours needed to meet them.

factCards.term: Four responsibilities of adolescents in the family
factCards.definition: Contributing to household tasks, managing their own schoolwork, respecting family rules and privacy, and making responsible decisions within agreed limits.

factCards.term: Two common forms of role conflict
factCards.definition: Work-family conflict, between paid employment and parenting, and role overload, where there are too many roles for the time available.

factCards.term: Three factors that alter a member's role over the life cycle
factCards.definition: Age, health and the number of dependants in the household.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which the roles of family members have changed in recent times.
questions.model: Any three, each with a brief explanation. Women's increased participation in paid employment means that domestic roles and childcare are shared more between partners, or handled by paid services. Smaller families and later childbearing mean parents give each child more time and money. Rising housing and childcare costs mean many households need two incomes, so the provider role is shared by both partners.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the roles and responsibilities of family members change through the family life cycle, and analyse the social and economic factors that have changed these roles.
questions.model: Life cycle: couples share household tasks; during childbearing and child-rearing, parents carry the provider, nurturing, educating, socialising and protecting roles; adolescents take on household tasks and gradual independence while parents move towards guidance; launching brings a shift to advice from a distance; in later life older members may need care and adult children take on practical and financial support. Social factors: more women in paid work, growth of lone-parent and smaller families, later marriage and childbearing, and acceptance of cohabitation and blended families. Economic factors: rising housing, childcare and education costs require two incomes, longer working hours reduce time for household tasks, and labour-saving appliances allow tasks to be divided differently. Full marks need the stages in order, a role or responsibility at each stage, and at least one social and one economic factor explained with its effect on roles.
